profiles.meeting_scenario: An internal troubleshooting meeting in an ML theory-and-systems research lab after repeated failures to reproduce a paper's empirical section on numerical instability in backpropagation. The team has a PyTorch implementation intended to show that, under floating-point training, deep ReLU networks rarely sustain superlinear growth in affine pieces during gradient descent, but the latest runs show inconsistent conclusions across machines: one set of runs suggests the affine-piece count plateaus early, while another appears to show continued growth in deeper models. The agenda is to diagnose why the empirical results are diverging, decide what the most plausible root cause is, and agree on a concrete fix for the next reproduction batch. The expected outcome is a shared troubleshooting plan for rerunning the experiment with a corrected setup and a short note on what evidence will count as the issue being fixed.

members.name: Dr. Lina Voss
members.expertise: theory-grounded empirical studies of optimization, numerical analysis in deep learning, reproducibility design
members.background: Lina leads the lab's effort on connecting approximation theory claims to practical gradient-based training behavior; she routinely designs the empirical protocols used to support theoretical papers and has strong intuitions about failure modes caused by precision and initialization details.
members.private_state: She wants the troubleshooting discussion to converge quickly on a minimally invasive rerun plan that preserves comparability with the draft paper's existing figures, and she is worried that changing too much of the pipeline will make prior results unusable.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the run is 'stable,' they mean the training dynamics are numerically well-behaved enough that gradient signs and activation patterns are not being corrupted by floating-point effects, even if the loss still decreases.
The 'piece count' used in discussion refers to the post-training estimate computed from the fixed 1D probe sweep script used for the paper figures, not an online or layerwise proxy.

If two runs use the same random seed and nominal architecture, then differences across machines are most likely due to precision mode or kernel-level arithmetic behavior rather than data-order effects.
A 'rerun with the same setup' naturally includes preserving the original logging cadence and probe grid because those are part of the experimental definition, not incidental instrumentation.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: PyTorch training pipelines, CUDA performance, experiment orchestration, metric logging
members.background: Arjun maintains the codebase and cluster jobs for the lab's large reproduction sweeps; he recently optimized the experiment scripts to reduce runtime and memory by changing logging behavior and enabling mixed-precision defaults on newer GPUs.
members.private_state: He wants to avoid a broad rollback of his pipeline changes and hopes to frame the issue as a measurement or instrumentation inconsistency rather than a training-core bug, since a full audit would delay several queued experiments.
hidden_assumptions: When people say the run is 'stable,' they mean there are no NaNs, no exploding loss, and the optimizer reaches a smooth decreasing trajectory.

The 'piece count' in conversation refers to the online metric logged every 500 steps from sampled activation-pattern changes on minibatches, because that is the operational signal available during training.

The recent discrepancy is probably tied to which 'deep sweep' checkpoint bundle people are looking at, since he assumes everyone knows the January jobs used the updated logging and AMP path while the December bundle did not.

A 'rerun with the same setup' means keeping the current orchestration stack and reproducing only the scientific knobs (seed list, architecture, optimizer), while implementation details like probe resolution and logging frequency are just engineering conveniences.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a 'stable' training run
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they need to check whether the deep runs are 'stable.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means numerically faithful backpropagation where finite-precision error is not qualitatively altering gradient directions or ReLU region transitions relevant to affine-piece growth.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means operational training stability: no NaNs/infs, bounded gradients, and monotone-ish loss reduction under the existing training loop.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML practice, 'stable training' is a familiar phrase that usually does not trigger clarification; both can discuss clipping, loss curves, and precision without noticing they are using different standards for the same word.

misalignment_points.topic: Which 'piece count' metric they are troubleshooting
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer to 'the piece count' when comparing discrepant results.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is thinking of the offline affine-piece estimate computed after training by sweeping a fixed 16,384-point 1D input grid through the final network, which is what appears in the draft figures.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is thinking of the online proxy logged during training, based on minibatch activation-pattern transitions every 500 optimizer steps, which he added to monitor runs cheaply.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both metrics are used inside the same project to talk about network linear-region complexity, and the online proxy was introduced as a convenience rather than a headline methodological change, so the phrase sounds safely shared.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both mention results from 'the deep sweep' as if it were one agreed experiment set.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 presupposes 'the deep sweep' means the December reproduction batch on A100 GPUs in full FP32 using the original paper script for depths 24, 32, and 40.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 presupposes 'the deep sweep' means the January rerun on H100 GPUs with autocast enabled by default and lighter logging, covering the same nominal depths.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The experiment names and folder labels are nearly identical, both cover the same depth settings, and both participants believe the shared shorthand has already been established in prior team discussions.

misalignment_points.topic: Scope of 'same setup' for the rerun
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree to 'rerun the same setup with FP32.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes this includes restoring the original full protocol: FP32 forward/backward, original probe grid density, per-epoch checkpointing, and the exact post-hoc piece-count script so the rerun is comparable to the paper draft.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes this only changes arithmetic precision in the training loop while retaining the current streamlined logging, reduced probe grid, and sparse checkpoint schedule to save compute.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'same setup' usually feels like a conservative agreement, and both regard their omitted details as background implementation choices rather than substantive parts of the experiment definition.

turns.inner_thought: We need to get this back onto a narrow track fast. The draft figures use the fixed post-training 1D probe sweep, and if we start changing instrumentation or protocol details, we'll lose comparability. What bothers me is that these deep runs don't look stable in the numerical sense: if finite precision is flipping gradient signs or changing ReLU region transitions, then the whole affine-piece story gets distorted even if the loss still goes down.

turns.inner_thought: From my side these jobs look stable enough: no NaNs, no infs, gradients bounded, loss coming down smoothly. I really don't want this to turn into a broad audit of the training core when the more likely issue is that people are comparing different piece count traces or different bundles. The online metric is exactly where I see the discrepancy.
turns.utterance: From the logs, the runs look stable overall to me—no NaNs, loss decays smoothly, nothing obviously blowing up. The odd part is really the piece count curves.

turns.utterance: Right, and in the deep sweep the piece count should have flattened by depth 32. So I want to understand why those curves now seem to keep climbing.

turns.inner_thought: I've already looked at gradient norms and loss traces; by my definition the training is stable. I want to keep the focus on measurement. turns.utterance: Okay, then let's pull one representative run from the deep sweep and recompute the final piece count on the standard 1D probe sweep. That should tell us whether the apparent growth is real.

turns.utterance: That's fine as long as we rerun the same setup with FP32 so we can compare directly to the figures already in the draft.
